lines.text: Office supplies — the everyday tools of professional life — carry a surprisingly rich vocabulary in English. Writing instruments include ballpoint pens, fountain pens, felt-tip markers, highlighters, and mechanical pencils. Paper products encompass notebooks, notepads, sticky notes (Post-its), index cards, envelopes, and letterheads. Filing and organisation rely on ring binders, lever arch files, folders, dividers, paper clips, bulldog clips, staples, and rubber bands. Adhesives include glue sticks, sticky tape (Sellotape in British English, Scotch tape in American), and correction fluid (Tipp-Ex in Britain, Wite-Out in America). Cutting tools range from scissors to craft knives and paper trimmers. Desktop accessories include pen holders, desk organisers, mouse mats, monitor stands, and cable tidies. The stationery cupboard — that shared resource guarded with varying degrees of strictness — is a feature of every British office. Digital tools have replaced many physical supplies: cloud storage instead of filing cabinets, digital signatures instead of stamps, shared documents instead of photocopies. Yet paper persists: diaries, planners, wall calendars, and the humble notebook remain essential for many workers. British and American vocabulary differs notably: 'rubber' (eraser) versus 'eraser', 'drawing pin' versus 'thumbtack', 'Sellotape' versus 'Scotch tape'. These small differences matter in professional communication.

lines.text: British people have a notable affection for stationery. Shops like Paperchase and sections in WHSmith attract devoted customers. 'Stationery haul' videos are popular online. A new notebook or quality pen brings genuine joy — it's a minor cultural phenomenon.

lines.text: Several office supply brand names have become generic in British English: 'Sellotape' (any sticky tape), 'Tipp-Ex' (any correction fluid), 'Biro' (any ballpoint pen), 'Post-it' (any sticky note). Using these shows cultural fluency.
lines.name: Several office supply brand names have become generic in British English: 'Sellotape' (any sticky tape), 'Tipp-Ex' (any correction fluid), 'Biro' (any ballpoint pen), 'Post-it' (any sticky note). Using these shows cultural fluency.

lines.text: The office stationery cupboard occupies a special place in British workplace culture. It may be locked (with the key held by the office manager), rationed ('only two pens per person'), or a source of gentle office politics ('who keeps taking all the good pens?').

lines.text: Despite the 'paperless office' dream, British workplaces still use significant paper. The phrase 'Can you print that out for me?' remains common, and many people prefer physical notebooks for meetings. The UK uses A4 paper (not US Letter size).

lines.text: In British English, 'rubber' = eraser. In American English, 'rubber' is slang for condom — a highly embarrassing false friend. Always use 'eraser' with American speakers.

lines.text: 'Staple' works as a verb — no need to mention the stapler. If you do, just say 'stapler' (not 'stapler machine'). Similarly: 'she photocopied it' (not 'used the photocopy machine').
